creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Signal Processing
FIR Filter Design
Window Method
Frequency Sampling Method
Parks-McClellan
dublinCore.description: Two linear-phase FIR filters designed for the same low-pass, high-pass or band-pass specification by the window method (rectangular, Hann, Hamming, Blackman or Kaiser), frequency sampling with a transition sample, or Parks-McClellan, overlaid with their impulse responses, zeros, phase or group delay and measured transition width, passband ripple and stop-band attenuation.
relation: Chapter 10: Advanced Filter Design and Implementation

learningObjectives: Apply the window method to design a low-pass, high-pass or band-pass FIR filter and read its transition width, passband ripple and stop-band attenuation
Compare how the rectangular, Hann, Hamming, Blackman and Kaiser windows trade transition width against stop-band attenuation at a fixed number of taps
Predict the stop-band attenuation and transition width of a Kaiser-window design from beta and N with Kaiser's formulas, and check the prediction against the measurement
Explain how the transition sample T1 changes the stop-band attenuation of a frequency-sampling design, and find the value that maximizes it
Evaluate which design method meets a given specification with the fewest taps, using Parks-McClellan as the optimal benchmark
prerequisites: z-transform and frequency response of an FIR filter
Ideal low-pass (sinc) impulse response and the DFT

misconceptions.misconception: More taps give more stop-band attenuation
misconceptions.correction: With the window method the window shape sets the attenuation; the number of taps sets the transition width
misconceptions.evidence: A Hamming design stays between 53.6 and 53.9 dB from N = 21 to N = 101 while the transition width shrinks from 0.333 pi to 0.067 pi

misconceptions.misconception: A frequency-sampling filter equals the ideal response because it matches it at every sample
misconceptions.correction: It matches only at w_k = 2 pi k / N; between the samples the response ripples
misconceptions.evidence: With T1 = 0 the samples are exactly 1 and 0, yet the passband ripple is 2.29 dB and the stop band rises to -16.4 dB

accessibility.screenReaderScript: FIR filter design comparison. Two designs, A (solid blue) and B (dashed maroon), meet the same low-pass, high-pass or band-pass cutoff. Each uses the window method, frequency sampling or Parks-McClellan with its own number of taps. The left plot shows the impulse response (or the zeros, phase or group delay); the right plot shows the magnitude response with the ideal response in grey. A table reports each design's transition width, passband ripple and stop-band attenuation.

model.description: Designs odd-length symmetric FIR filters by the window method, frequency sampling (inverse DFT of amplitude samples with a transition sample) or the Parks-McClellan Remez exchange, evaluates |H| at 2049 frequencies and measures ripple, attenuation and transition width.
equations: h[n] = (1/N) [A_0 + 2 sum_{k=1}^{M} A_k cos(2 pi k (n - M) / N)]
Ripple = 20 log10((1 + dp)/(1 - dp)), As = -20 log10(ds)
algorithms: Window method (rectangular, Hann, Hamming, Blackman, Kaiser)
Frequency sampling with one transition sample
Parks-McClellan / Remez exchange with barycentric interpolation
Aberth-Ehrlich polynomial root finding for the zeros
limitations: Parks-McClellan uses equal pass-band and stop-band weights
The Parks-McClellan transition width is narrowed when Kaiser's estimate exceeds 130 dB or when a band would lose more than half its width
Only odd N (type I linear phase) is supported

instructionalStrategies: Fill in a window comparison table at fixed N
Predict with Kaiser's formulas, then verify
Find the fewest taps that meet a specification with each method
extensions: Add unequal pass-band and stop-band weights to the Parks-McClellan design
Add even-length (type II) designs and compare their high-pass behavior
